brief: An extreme overhead crop down into a full glass of red wine, so the liquid fills the frame like a colour-field canvas. Vast soaked fields of garnet, prune and rose-madder watercolour bleed into one another with soft, haloed stain edges. Where the meniscus meets glass, a single hairline arc of startling white highlight and a refracted sliver of tablecloth snap into hyperreal focus. Tiny tear-drop legs drip down the inside wall at one edge. The surface is mostly meditative, unmodulated stain, with realism concentrated in a few precise reflections.

A half-unwrapped deli sandwich in crinkled waxed paper on a stainless counter. The interest is translucency: lettuce, pastrami and mustard seen hazily through the waxy layers, with sharp clarity where grease spots turn the paper clear. The image is built from soft pencil underdrawing veiled by milky, semi-opaque white glazes layered thinly, with crisp creases catching hard fluorescent highlights. The palette is pale and muted: bone, smoked salmon pink, mustard ochre and a faint cool steel. The edges are soft and fogged under the paper and razor-sharp where the sandwich escapes it.

A wedge of watermelon resting on a dusty sky-blue car hood at dusk, framed inside a thick off-white instant-film border with a wider lower margin. The image inside carries instant-film chemistry: a cyan-green shadow cast, warm magenta-blown highlights and softened focus fall-off. Faint sprayed emulsion blooms and a chemical streak creep in from one edge. The seeds, wet flesh and hood paint are photoreal but slightly overexposed. The border itself is drawn crisply in pencil, with a thumbprint smudge and a faint handwritten scrawl suggested in marker.

A strictly frontal elevation of a modernist student dormitory: a rigid grid of steel-framed windows set in white render, cropped edge to edge with no sky. Each pane is a hyperreal vignette seen through glass. One holds a chipped mug on a sill, one a drooping towel, one a reflected cloud, one a desk lamp, one a half-drawn blind. The window mullions are drawn in precise ruled pen, and the panes are glazed in cool graphite-grey watercolour. Exactly one pane glows signal orange from a lamp behind a curtain. The mood is flat and orderly.

Spilled black coffee spreading across a white paper napkin on a pale ash café table, seen from above. The absorption front is painted as nested isochrone bands. Each ring of wicking is a distinct watercolour wash, stepping outward from espresso umber through burnt sienna to the faintest tea-stain amber, each with a hard tide-line edge. The napkin's embossed quilting pattern is drawn in fine pencil and distorts the bands. A tipped cup and a glossy pooled puddle remain photoreal at the source. The bands thin into dry fibre at the edges.

A round dinner table photographed straight down after a meal, organised as a T-O world map. A runner and a spilled wine trail divide the circle into three continents of plates, bones, bread crusts and crumpled napkins. The parchment-toned watercolour ground carries hyperreal wine rings, gravy smears and candle wax. A ring of iron-gall brown pen frames the table like an encircling ocean. Faint marginalia doodles in sepia sit in the corners. The palette is vellum, oxblood, verdigris and lamp-black. Soft candlelight falls warm from one side.

An airport baggage reclaim arranged as Egyptian tomb registers. Three horizontal bands are separated by ruled ochre lines, and in each a conveyor carries suitcases, a duffel, a pram and a cardboard box in strict side profile, marching left to right. Each item is hyperreal: scuffed polycarbonate, zip teeth, tangled luggage tags, peeling stickers. The ground is a warm limestone-plaster watercolour wash with flaking edges. The limited tomb palette is red ochre, Egyptian blue, malachite green, carbon black and gypsum white. Neat columns of tiny pictographic marks label each piece.

A single floating isometric slab of city sidewalk, cut cleanly out of the world like a game tile, hovering on a flat pale lilac void. On it, rendered with obsessive realism: a paint-chipped fire hydrant, a flattened gum blot, a hairline crack sprouting moss, three wet plane-tree leaves and a bottle cap. The slab's cut sides show strata of concrete, gravel and soil. The texture comes from fine pen stippling over transparent watercolour glazes. All shadows fall to the same isometric diagonal. The edges are razor-straight against the soft, empty ground.

A close crop of a human forearm with a just-finished American traditional panther tattoo, still wrapped in cling film. The flash itself has bold black pen outlines, flat scarlet, canary yellow and jade fills, and dotted whip-shading. Around it, the hyperreal skin carries pores, fine hairs, angry pink inflammation and beads of plasma and ink trapped under the wrinkled plastic. The film's specular creases are lifted out in sharp white. The background is a dim, out-of-focus studio of brown leather. The contrast is between graphic flatness and wet, living surface.

A half-drop wallpaper repeat in which soft, salt-crusted pretzels interlock like a Morris trellis. Between them twist hyperreal knotted bread rolls and scattered caraway seeds where leaves would be. Each pretzel is photoreal: glossy lye-browned crust, cracked splits showing pale dough, and coarse salt crystals with tiny cast shadows. The ground is a block-printed flat of indigo and madder brown with slightly broken ink coverage and occasional off-register slips. The pattern runs edge to edge with no focal point, so the realism repeats rhythmically.

A raw, heavily marbled ribeye lies on creased pink butcher paper, seen from directly overhead and filling most of the frame. The intramuscular fat is painted wet-in-wet like Calacatta veining. Branching ivory rivulets bleed softly into the alizarin and madder-carmine muscle, with crisp granulating edges where the paint dried. Glistening moisture is rendered with lifted highlights. A faint pink blood seep wicks into the paper fibres. Pencil grain describes the paper's crumpled ridges. The light is cool and diffuse, like a butcher's chiller cabinet, with no drama and only clinical candour.

A tight detail of a parked car's side mirror fills the panel, in the jewel-like manner of a Flemish altarpiece. Inside the convex glass, an entire miniature street bends around: a cyclist, a bakery awning, a woman with a pram and the painter's own tiny figure. Each is rendered with tiny pen strokes and fine glazes. The mirror's housing is lacquered oxblood red, its gloss built through many thin transparent washes. Rain-spotted dust sits on the plastic rim. The palette is deep, saturated and luminous: carmine, verdigris and lead-white highlights. The finish is meticulous and devotional, held to a single fixed eye.

A dented silver-gilt bowling trophy is seen from below, filling the frame like a monument. Its surface is half tarnished: bloom-patches of bruised purple, smoky brown and blue-black graphite gather in the engraved scrolls. Worn high points show through as warm gilt in muted yellow ochre and old brass. Smudged adult fingerprints cloud the cup's belly, every whorl rendered. A distorted reflection of a wood-panelled clubhouse wraps around the curve. The medium is dense charcoal and graphite tonal work with restrained watercolour glazes for the gilt. The background is a dim, out-of-focus amber haze.

A chaekgeori scholar's bookshelf screen is reimagined with today's possessions, rendered hyperreal. Stacked compartments, drawn in tilted reverse perspective, hold instant ramen packets, a game controller, a soju bottle, glasses on folded comics and a potted orchid in a celadon pot. Each item is rendered with exact labels and gloss. The shelving itself is flat and folk-like, outlined in fine ink and filled with mineral watercolour in cinnabar, malachite green, azurite and ochre on aged mulberry-paper tone. The grid fills the whole sheet with no single focal point. It is cheerful, auspicious and quietly witty.

A hyperreal opened tin of corned beef sits at the centre of a beaten bark-cloth field. The whole surface has the felted, fibrous grain of mulberry bark, shown with dry hatching in raw sienna and buff. The ground is divided into ruled panels of hand-stamped geometric bands, triangles, chevrons and stars, in burnt umber and lamp black. The ink is slightly uneven, as if rubbed on. The tin itself is painstakingly realistic, with a curling peeled lid, a glint of tinplate, marbled pink meat and a waxy fat sheen. The flat ornament and the illusionistic object sit in deliberate tension, and the frontal, symmetrical layout feels ceremonial.

A smartphone lies face-up on a slate-grey kitchen counter, its screen shattered in a spiderweb fracture radiating from one corner. Each crack is filled with raised gold seams in warm yellow ochre, lit with pale highlights and drawn in confident fine pen and marker. Beneath the broken glass, a hyperreal lock-screen photo of a child at the beach glows in soft watercolour. Its blues and peaches are cut and offset slightly where the shards shift. Dust, fingerprint smears and the rubber case's worn edge are exact. The view is a close, slightly oblique top-down shot. The feeling is of damage honoured rather than hidden.

A cream rotary telephone sits on a lacquered side table, its receiver dangling by a taut coiled cord. It is lit by violent coloured gels: one side drenched in hot magenta, the other in acid cyan, meeting in a bruised violet seam. A black leather glove rests beside the dial, its creases hyperreal. The shadows are deep and inky, laid with soft spray mist over hard marker edges, giving a cinematic grain. Reflections of the gels slide along the bakelite gloss. The camera angle is low and canted. A fragment of patterned wallpaper looms behind, and the mood is suspense frozen mid-breath.

The tarred, weathered oak bow of a clinker-built fishing boat pulled up on a Norwegian shingle beach, every plank lap and iron rivet exact. The marks follow the logic of carving. Dense sepia pen hatching runs strictly along the wood grain like gouge cuts, and curls into knots and interlaced spirals where the grain swirls. Thin raw-umber and tar-black washes sit underneath. Salt crust and lichen are flecked in pale grey. The prow rises steeply, cropped at the top, and the composition is a tall vertical with strong carved rhythm.

A crowded, loud tabletop sits under hard noon light. A hyperreal bunch of bananas with bruised speckled skins lies draped over a chrome-and-red transistor radio. Next to them are a sweating glass bottle of guaraná, a plastic parrot and a scrap of a green-and-yellow flag. The colour is saturated and joyful, almost clashing: banana yellow, parrot green, cobalt, lipstick red and bubblegum pink. It is laid down in dense alcohol-marker layering that keeps crisp hard-edged shadows. The background is a pop cut-out of stylised giant tropical leaves, flat and graphic. Exact realism collides with kitsch collage.

A heavy cut-crystal tumbler of amber whisky sits on a dark walnut bar. Floating in it is a single large ice cube with an orange marigold frozen at its core. The flower is fractured by refraction: petals doubled, warped, and split by the cube's internal fissures and trapped bubble trails. The whole is drawn in sharp coloured pencil over layered watercolour in honey, cadmium orange and cold blue-white. The glass facets throw prismatic slivers onto the wood. Condensation crawls down the tumbler. The view is low and side-on, with warm bar light from behind. It feels slow and luxurious.
